note: Group hub pages (web/tool-docs, 'Domain and group index pages'): the tasks a group's tools serve, each tool in exactly one task, and a short guide where the tools form a sequence. Tool ids are the operation within the group, or a full id for a tool elsewhere. Unit groups need no entry: their one task is converting.

aviation.intro: Aviation calculators for pilots planning a flight: altimetry, the standard atmosphere, airspeed, wind, weight and balance, fuel, performance, IFR holding and DME geometry, and plain-language weather decoding. Each tool shows its method and sources under "How we got this," with the common rule of thumb beside the exact answer. A good place to start is the METAR decoder, then density altitude and runway wind components for the departure. These are planning and education aids: your POH or AFM, current charts, and ATC govern.

aviation.airspace.summary: Airspace from NOTAM text: TFR circles and areas with their limits.
aviation.airspace.intro: Draws the area a TFR or NOTAM describes, from a circle around a point or fix to a list of corner points, with its altitude limits, and lets you download it as GeoJSON. Pilots and drone operators use it to see where a restriction sits before a flight. Start with the TFR and NOTAM area tool and paste the coordinates as the NOTAM gives them. It draws only what you enter, so check the drawing against the official NOTAM text before you rely on it.

tasks.want: draw a TFR or NOTAM area and download it

aviation.airspeed.summary: From the number on the airspeed indicator to true airspeed and Mach, and back.
aviation.airspeed.intro: Turns the number on the airspeed indicator into calibrated airspeed, true airspeed, and Mach, and works back from a true airspeed or Mach to the calibrated airspeed to fly. Pilots use it for flight planning, the wind triangle, and checking cruise performance. Start with the true airspeed tool, which shows the 2% per 1,000 ft rule beside the exact answer. Correct indicated airspeed to calibrated first, from the calibration table in your POH or AFM, because the rest of the chain assumes calibrated airspeed.

tasks.want: turn indicated or calibrated airspeed into true airspeed and Mach
find the calibrated airspeed to fly for a true airspeed or Mach
get outside air temperature from a total air temperature probe

steps.text: IAS is what the airspeed indicator shows. Correcting it for instrument and position error, from the calibration table in the POH or AFM, gives calibrated airspeed (CAS).
Correcting CAS for the compression of air in the pitot tube gives equivalent airspeed (EAS). The difference is small below about 200 kt and 10,000 ft and grows with speed and altitude.
Correcting EAS for air density, from pressure altitude and outside air temperature, gives true airspeed (TAS): your speed through the air mass.
TAS divided by the local speed of sound, which depends only on temperature, is the Mach number. A probe reads total air temperature, warmer than the outside air at speed, so convert it first.
To plan the other way, from a TAS or Mach you want to the CAS to fly, run the chain in reverse.

aviation.altimetry.summary: Pressure altitude, the standard temperature for it, density altitude, and cold-day corrections.
aviation.altimetry.intro: Pressure altitude, the standard temperature for it, density altitude, flight levels, the QNH, QFE, and QNE settings, and cold-temperature corrections. Pilots use these tools before a hot or high departure, when planning a flight level, and when flying approaches on a cold day. Start with pressure altitude, then carry it into density altitude. Remember that the altimeter reads correctly only in standard temperatures: in cold air you are lower than it shows, which the cold temperature tool corrects for.

tasks.want: convert between QNH and QFE, or work out the altimeter setting
find the lowest usable flight level or a flight level's altitude
correct approach altitudes for a cold day
find my true altitude in cold or warm air
find pressure altitude from field elevation and the altimeter setting
know how far today's temperature is from standard
find density altitude for takeoff and climb performance

steps.text: Start from field elevation and the altimeter setting: the difference from 29.92 inHg (1013.25 hPa) gives pressure altitude.
The standard atmosphere gives the temperature expected at that pressure altitude; the deviation says how much warmer or colder today is.
Pressure altitude and outside air temperature give density altitude, the altitude the airplane performs as if it were at.

aviation.atmosphere.summary: Pressure, temperature, density, and speed of sound in the standard atmosphere.
aviation.atmosphere.intro: The ICAO standard atmosphere at any altitude, humidity and dew point relations, and estimates of cloud base and freezing level. Pilots use it to see how far today's air is from standard and to judge where cumulus clouds will form. Start with the standard atmosphere tool for pressure, temperature, and density at a height. The standard atmosphere is a reference model, not a forecast, and the cloud base from the temperature and dew point spread is an estimate for well-mixed air, not a report.

tasks.want: work out humidity, dew point, and moist air density
look up the standard atmosphere at an altitude
estimate the cloud base and freezing level

aviation.ifr.summary: Holding, DME, and station geometry for instrument flying.
aviation.ifr.intro: Holding entries, holding speeds and wind correction, DME slant range and arcs, radial fixes and intercepts, and time to a station, for instrument pilots planning or reviewing a procedure. Start with the holding entry tool, which picks direct, teardrop, or parallel from your heading and the hold's inbound course, per AIM 5-3-8. Decide the entry from your heading as you reach the fix, not from where you are when the clearance comes. ATC instructions and the published procedure always govern.

tasks.want: choose a holding entry
know the maximum holding airspeed
correct a hold for wind and time the legs
find the fix on a radial at a distance, with the station's variation
turn a DME reading into ground distance
time a bearing change to find the station
find the lead points for a DME arc
find the heading to intercept a radial

aviation.loading.summary: Fuel planning with legal reserves, fuel weight, and weight and balance.
aviation.loading.intro: Weight and balance, fuel weight, fuel planning with the legal reserve, weight shifts, ballast, and reading a POH performance table between its printed values. Pilots use these tools before every flight where weight or fuel is close. Start with weight and balance, which checks your center of gravity against your envelope at takeoff and after the fuel burn. Check both: burning fuel moves the CG, and a load that is in limits for takeoff can be out of limits for landing.

tasks.want: plan fuel for a trip, with the legal reserve
turn fuel volume into weight
check weight and center of gravity
see where the CG goes when I move weight, or how much to move
find the ballast that brings the CG into limits
read a POH performance table between its values

aviation.performance.summary: Climb, descent, glide, turns, and range per gallon.
aviation.performance.intro: Climb gradient and vertical speed, top of descent, the visual descent point, glide range with wind, turn radius and load factor, pivotal altitude, and range per gallon. Pilots use these tools for departure climb requirements, descent planning, and emergency glide planning. Start with top of descent, which shows the 3-to-1 and 5 times groundspeed rules beside the exact values. Both rules start you down a little late and descend a little slowly, so on a long descent they leave you high.

tasks.want: know how far each gallon takes me
plan a climb gradient or vertical speed
plan when to start down
know how far I can glide
work out a turn: radius, rate, bank, and load factor

aviation.weather.summary: METARs, TAFs, and winds aloft, decoded into plain language.
aviation.weather.intro: Decoders for METARs, TAFs, and FB winds and temperatures aloft, turning the coded text into plain language with each group explained. Pilots use them during preflight briefings and to check a report they are not sure how to read. Start with the METAR decoder, then carry its wind, temperature, and altimeter setting into the wind and altimetry tools. Remember that winds in METARs, TAFs, and forecasts aloft are from true north, while ATIS and tower winds are magnetic.

tasks.want: read a METAR or TAF
read a winds aloft forecast

aviation.wind.summary: The wind triangle and runway wind components.
aviation.wind.intro: The wind triangle in every direction, runway headwind and crosswind components, ranking runways for a wind, winds aloft between forecast levels, true course to compass heading, and the 1-in-60 rule for getting back on course. Pilots use these tools for cross-country planning and runway choice. Start with heading and groundspeed, the wind side of the E6B solved exactly. Work in one reference: forecast winds are true, runways and ATIS winds are magnetic, so convert before you compare.

tasks.want: find the heading to fly and my groundspeed
work out the wind from heading, track, and speeds
find the airspeed and heading for a groundspeed I need
see where a heading and airspeed will take me
find the headwind and crosswind on a runway
rank the runways for the wind
find the wind at my altitude between forecast levels
turn a wind into u and v components, or back
work out the compass heading from a true course
get back on course with the 1-in-60 rule

steps.text: Your airplane moves through the air on its heading at true airspeed; the air moves over the ground with the wind. Adding the two gives your track and groundspeed.
In flight, a known heading, track, TAS, and groundspeed give the wind back.
At the runway, the same wind splits into a headwind and a crosswind component.

drone.intro: Calculators for planning drone work: mapping and photogrammetry, mission patterns, flight time and batteries, radio links, sensors, and the Part 107 and EASA open-category rules. They are for remote pilots, mapping crews, and anyone sizing a drone for a job. Most mapping jobs start with the GSD tool, then overlap and trigger, then the survey grid. These are planning aids: a flight still needs the current rules, any airspace authorization it requires, and your aircraft's own limits.

drone.links.summary: Radio links: path loss, fade margin, and the EIRP limit.
drone.links.intro: A link budget for a drone's control or video radio: free-space path loss, received signal, and fade margin over a distance, with the transmitter's EIRP checked against the dated 2.4 GHz limit where you fly. It is for pilots planning longer flights and builders choosing radios and antennas. Start with the link budget tool. Free-space loss is the best case: terrain, trees, buildings, and the ground near the path all cut the real range, so keep a generous fade margin.

tasks.want: work out a radio link budget and check the EIRP limit

drone.mission.summary: Flight patterns for mapping and inspection.
drone.mission.intro: Flight patterns for mapping and inspection: a serpentine survey grid over an area, corridor lines along a road or pipeline, an orbit around a tower, facade passes up a wall, a geofence, and waypoint export as KML, GeoJSON, or CSV. It is for mapping and inspection pilots. Start with the survey grid for an area map, using the line and photo spacing from the overlap and trigger tool. Check the height reference before you fly: a constant height above takeoff is not a constant height above the ground, and overlap drops over hills.

tasks.want: lay out a mapping grid over an area
map a road, pipeline, or river
circle a point of interest
photograph a building face
fence a mission and check its waypoints
save waypoints as KML, GeoJSON, or CSV

drone.ops.summary: Rules checks for Part 107 and the EASA open category.
drone.ops.intro: Rules checks for flying under Part 107 in the United States and the EASA open category in Europe: the 400 ft altitude limit and its structure exception, the 87 knot groundspeed limit, which open subcategory a drone fits, and impact energy against the published thresholds. It is for remote pilots checking a plan against the rules. Start with the Part 107 altitude tool. Each tool checks one rule; none grants airspace access, and a waiver, a TFR, or controlled airspace can change what you may fly.

tasks.want: check an altitude or speed limit under Part 107
find my EASA open subcategory
know the impact energy of my drone

steps.text: Civil twilight under §107.29(c) is the 30 minutes after official sunset and before official sunrise (the Air Almanac period in Alaska); the four-nights tool shows it for your site and date, with when §1.1 night begins.
In civil twilight and at night the drone needs anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles; at night the remote pilot also needs the §107.65 training.
The altitude limit is the same at dusk as by day.

drone.photogrammetry.summary: Ground sampling distance, overlap, image count, blur, and accuracy.
drone.photogrammetry.intro: The numbers behind a mapping flight: ground sample distance, the height for a target GSD, overlap, trigger interval and line spacing, image count, motion blur, overlap over high ground, oblique footprints, and accuracy to the ASPRS Edition 2 standard. It is for drone mapping crews and surveyors planning photogrammetry. Start with the GSD tool, then overlap and trigger. Use the camera's physical focal length, not the 35 mm equivalent on the spec sheet, or the GSD comes out far too fine.

tasks.want: find the GSD for a height, or the height for a GSD
find the GSD and footprint of a tilted (oblique) camera
check overlap where the ground rises
set overlap, trigger interval, and line spacing
estimate how many images a job takes
check for motion blur
state accuracy to the ASPRS standard

steps.text: Pick the ground sampling distance the deliverable needs, and find the height that gives it with your camera.
Choose front and side overlap; they set the photo interval and the spacing between lines.
Check the shutter speed keeps motion blur under a fraction of a pixel at your groundspeed.
Estimate the image count for the area, which drives batteries and processing time.
After processing, report accuracy against checkpoints to the ASPRS standard.

drone.power.summary: Battery energy, hover power, flight time, and reserves.
drone.power.intro: Battery energy, multirotor hover power, flight time, return-to-home reserves, and payload limits, worked out from the battery label and the aircraft's mass. It is for pilots and builders estimating how long a drone can fly and what a payload costs. Start with battery energy, then flight time. The estimates are only as good as the power figure: wind, climbs, cold, and aging packs all shorten real flight time, so calibrate hover power from your own test flight when you can.

tasks.want: turn a battery's mAh and voltage into watt-hours
estimate flight time
keep enough energy to come home
find how much payload I can carry
see what a payload costs in flight time
tune the power estimate to my own aircraft

guide.title: From battery label to flight time

steps.text: A battery's capacity in mAh times its voltage is its energy in watt-hours.
Hover power depends on weight and rotor area; flight time is usable energy over power.
Hold back what the return leg needs, against the wind.

drone.sensors.summary: Lidar flight planning, thermal pixel footprints, how much storage a mapping job needs, and how far away a drone stays visible.
drone.sensors.intro: Sensor planning beyond the camera: lidar swath and point density against the USGS 3DEP quality levels, the storage a mapping job needs, a thermal camera's pixel footprint and smallest measurable target, and how far a drone stays in visual line of sight. It is for crews flying lidar, thermal, and mapping payloads. Start with the tool for your sensor. The line-of-sight tool uses EASA guidance formulas for planning; it cannot promise you will see the aircraft against a bright sky or a busy background.

tasks.want: plan a lidar flight for a USGS quality level
estimate how much storage a mapping job needs
find a thermal camera's pixel footprint and smallest target
know how far I can see my drone

geodesy.intro: Geodesy is the math of where things are on the Earth: datums, heights, map projections, grid references, and the Earth's shape and magnetic field. These tools convert coordinates between systems, turn GPS heights into elevations, and write positions as UTM, state plane, or MGRS. Surveyors, GIS analysts, and developers use them to make data from different sources line up. If the terms are new, the Learn pages on datums and on geoid heights are a good first stop.

geodesy.datum.summary: Moving coordinates between datums, frames, and epochs.
geodesy.datum.intro: These tools move coordinates between datums, frames, and epochs: NAD 83, the ITRF, WGS 84, NAD 27 and other old datums, and legacy datums worldwide. Surveyors and GIS analysts use them when GNSS data meets older control or a map on a different datum. For modern GNSS positions in the US, start with the NAD 83 transformation. The common pitfall is treating NAD 83(2011) and WGS 84 as the same, which puts a meter or more of error in the data.

tasks.want: move coordinates between NAD 83, ITRF, and WGS 84
bring an old US datum to NAD 83
convert a legacy datum to or from WGS 84
apply a Helmert transformation I have the parameters for
move a position to another epoch

geodesy.ellipsoid.summary: Ellipsoid parameters, radii, and auxiliary latitudes.
geodesy.ellipsoid.intro: These tools describe the reference ellipsoid itself: its axes, flattening, and mean radii, its radii of curvature at a latitude, and the auxiliary latitudes used inside map projection and geodesic formulas. Developers and geodesy students use them to check constants and intermediate values. Start with the ellipsoid parameters for WGS 84 or GRS 80. One pitfall: the two ellipsoids differ slightly in flattening, so pick the one your datum actually uses.

tasks.want: look up an ellipsoid's parameters
find the radius of curvature or the length of a degree
convert between geodetic and other latitudes

geodesy.frame.intro: These tools convert between latitude, longitude, and height and Earth-centered X, Y, Z (ECEF), and between a point and a local east-north-up, north-east-down, or azimuth-elevation-range frame. Developers, drone and antenna engineers, and GNSS users need them to relate a position to where they stand. Start with latitude, longitude, and height to ECEF. The usual pitfall is feeding in a height above sea level; these frames need height above the ellipsoid.

tasks.want: convert between latitude, longitude, height and ECEF
describe a point from where I stand (ENU, NED, azimuth and elevation)

geodesy.geoid.summary: The geoid height that separates GPS heights from heights above sea level.
geodesy.geoid.intro: The geoid height is how far the geoid, close to mean sea level, sits above the ellipsoid that GPS heights refer to. Surveyors, drone pilots, and GIS analysts need it to turn a GPS height into an elevation. This group reads the global EGM96 model at any point. It is not NAVD 88: for official US elevations use NGS GEOID18.

tasks.want: find the geoid height at a point

geodesy.grid-ref.summary: Military, aviation, and radio grid references.
geodesy.grid-ref.intro: These tools write and read grid references: MGRS and the US National Grid, plus GARS, GEOREF, and Maidenhead locators. Search and rescue teams, military users, pilots, and radio amateurs use them to pass a position as a short code. Start with MGRS encoding for a point. The main pitfall is rounding a shortened reference; MGRS and USNG truncate, and a reference names a square, not a point.

tasks.want: convert to or from MGRS or USNG
convert to or from GARS or GEOREF
convert to or from a Maidenhead locator

geodesy.height.intro: This group converts between a GPS height above the ellipsoid, a height above mean sea level, and a height above the ground you give. Drone operators, surveyors, and GIS analysts use it to line up GPS heights with maps and terrain. Start with the height conversion. The classic mistake is reading a GPS height as elevation, which can be off by tens of meters: about 28 m in central Kansas.

tasks.want: turn a GPS height into a height above sea level, or back

geodesy.magnetic.summary: Magnetic declination and true and magnetic bearings.
geodesy.magnetic.intro: These tools give magnetic declination from the World Magnetic Model or IGRF, the angle from grid north to magnetic north, and conversions between true and magnetic bearings. Pilots, hikers, surveyors retracing old bearings, and drone operators calibrating compasses use them. Start with magnetic declination for your place and date. Declination changes year to year, so an old chart's variation or an old deed's bearing needs the date it was true.

tasks.want: find the magnetic declination
convert a bearing between true and magnetic
find the angle from grid north to magnetic north

geodesy.parse.summary: Reading, formatting, and comparing coordinates and bearings.
geodesy.parse.intro: These tools read and write coordinates and angles: decimal degrees, degrees-minutes-seconds, packed aviation formats, MGRS, and UTM, plus DMS arithmetic and the turn between two bearings. Anyone copying coordinates between systems uses them. Start with reading any coordinate, which reports what it assumed. The common pitfall is a longitude missing its west sign or W, which moves a US point to Asia.

tasks.want: read a coordinate in any notation
write a coordinate in another format
find the angle between two bearings
add or subtract angles in degrees, minutes, and seconds

geodesy.projection.summary: Map projections you set up yourself, and corrections for lines drawn on them.
geodesy.projection.intro: This group puts a latitude and longitude on a map grid whose parameters you give, and brings grid coordinates back. Use it when a grid is not UTM or State Plane: a web map, a national or regional conic, an equal-area map, or a polar grid. Each point comes with the grid convergence and the scale there. It also corrects a grid bearing for the curve of a long line. The pitfall is a parameter copied wrong, such as feet taken for meters, which gives a clean but wrong answer.

tasks.want: convert on a transverse Mercator grid other than UTM, like the British National Grid
put a point on a web map grid (EPSG:3857), or read one back
convert on a Lambert conformal conic grid you have the parameters for
convert on an equal-area grid, where areas stay true
convert on a polar grid other than UPS
convert on a plate carrée grid, where northing is distance from the equator
map true distances and directions from one place, like range rings
make shortest paths straight lines on the map
draw the Earth as a globe seen from space
convert on an oblique Mercator grid along a slanted band
correct a grid bearing for the curve of the projected line

geodesy.spcs.intro: These tools convert between NAD 83 latitude and longitude and State Plane Coordinate System of 1983 eastings and northings, and find which zone covers a place. US surveyors, engineers, and county GIS staff use them for deeds, plats, and project control. Start with the zone lookup, then convert. The costly pitfall is the foot: US survey feet and international feet differ by 2 parts per million, which is feet on a state plane coordinate.

tasks.want: find the state plane zone for a place
convert between latitude and longitude and state plane

steps.text: Find the zone for the job from the state and county, or from a point.
Convert latitude and longitude to northing and easting in that zone, in its legal unit.
Grid distances are not ground distances: the combined factor scales between them.

geodesy.ups.summary: Universal Polar Stereographic, for the polar caps UTM does not cover.
geodesy.ups.intro: Universal Polar Stereographic (UPS) is the grid for the polar caps, north of 84° N and south of 80° S, where UTM stops. Polar researchers, military users, and anyone mapping Antarctica or the high Arctic use it. Start with latitude and longitude to UPS. A pitfall is expecting a zone number: UPS has none, and in MGRS the polar areas use the letters A, B, Y, and Z instead.

tasks.want: convert to or from UPS

geodesy.utm.intro: These tools convert between latitude and longitude and Universal Transverse Mercator zone, easting, and northing, and find a point's zone and latitude band, including the Norway and Svalbard exceptions. GIS analysts, drone mappers, and field teams use UTM for measuring in meters. Start with UTM forward. The usual pitfall is dropping the zone or hemisphere, since the same numbers repeat in every zone.

tasks.want: find the UTM zone for a place
convert between latitude and longitude and UTM

geometry.intro: These tools measure and shape areas and lines on the real Earth, not on a flat map: polygon area, buffers, overlaps, point-in-polygon tests, simplification, and repairs. GIS analysts, developers, and drone mappers use them when a flat-map shortcut would bend the answer. Edges follow geodesics on the WGS 84 ellipsoid, and shapes that cross the antimeridian or circle a pole are handled. Start with polygon area.

geometry.area.intro: This group measures the area and perimeter of a polygon on the WGS 84 ellipsoid, with geodesic edges, holes, and shapes that cross the antimeridian or circle a pole. Farmers, land managers, GIS analysts, and drone mappers use it for field and parcel areas. Start with polygon area. The pitfall is computing area from raw latitude and longitude as if they were flat x and y; a degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles.

tasks.want: find the area and perimeter of a polygon

geometry.buffer.summary: Zones a set distance around points, lines, and polygons.
geometry.buffer.intro: This group draws the area within a set distance of a point, line, or polygon, measured on the ellipsoid, or shrinks a polygon inward. GIS analysts, planners, and drone operators use it for setbacks, geofences, and keep-out zones. Start with the geodesic buffer. One pitfall is buffering in degrees in a GIS package: a buffer of a fixed number of degrees is narrower east to west than north to south away from the equator.

tasks.want: draw a zone around a point, line, or polygon

geometry.distance.summary: How far apart lines and tracks are.
geometry.distance.intro: This group compares two tracks or routes as whole shapes: the Fréchet distance, the Hausdorff distance, and their closest approach. Developers, GPS track analysts, and researchers use it to tell whether two recorded paths follow the same route. Start with comparing two tracks. A pitfall is judging similarity by closest approach alone; two paths can touch once and still be far apart elsewhere.

tasks.want: compare two GPS tracks

geometry.mesh.summary: Triangles and nearest-point regions from scattered points.
geometry.mesh.intro: This group builds Delaunay triangles and Voronoi cells from a set of points, on a local flat map for a regional set or on the sphere for a global one. GIS analysts and developers use them for nearest-station areas, interpolation, and coverage maps. Start with Voronoi cells to see which point is nearest each place. The pitfall is triangulating global data on a flat map, which breaks at the antimeridian and near the poles.

tasks.want: triangulate survey or sensor points
find the region nearest each point

geometry.overlay.summary: Overlaps, unions, and differences of polygons.
geometry.overlay.intro: This group finds where two polygons overlap, their combined outline, and what one covers that the other does not, with geodesic areas. GIS analysts and drone operators use it to compare parcels, flight areas, and geofences. Start with the overlap of two polygons. A common pitfall is feeding in an invalid polygon, such as a bow-tie with crossed edges; check and repair it first.

tasks.want: find where two areas overlap, or combine or subtract them

geometry.predicate.summary: Tests of where points and shapes sit against each other.
geometry.predicate.intro: This group tests whether points fall inside a polygon with geodesic edges, including holes and points on the boundary, and how two shapes relate: whether they touch, cross, overlap, or lie one inside the other. Developers and GIS analysts use it for geofencing, assigning points to areas, and checking a route against a zone. Start with point in polygon. A pitfall is a long polygon edge drawn as a straight line on a flat map; on the Earth it bows, and points near it can change sides.

tasks.want: check whether points are inside a polygon
check whether a route or area touches, crosses, or lies inside another

geometry.shape.summary: Centers, interior points, and envelopes of shapes.
geometry.shape.intro: These tools describe a shape: its bounding box, centroid and a point guaranteed inside it, extra vertices along geodesic edges, and the hull, rectangle, and circle that enclose a set of points. GIS analysts and developers use them for map extents, labels, and summaries. Start with the bounding box. The classic pitfall is a box that crosses the antimeridian, where west is greater than east.

tasks.want: find a polygon's center or a point inside it
find the bounding box, even across the antimeridian
find the hull, smallest rectangle, or smallest circle around points
add vertices so a line follows the geodesic on a flat map

geometry.simplify.summary: Fewer vertices, with the shape kept.
geometry.simplify.intro: These tools remove vertices from a line or polygon while keeping it within a set tolerance, by the Douglas-Peucker or Visvalingam method, and report the largest deviation. Developers and cartographers use them to shrink GPS tracks and boundaries for faster maps. Start with Douglas-Peucker for a distance tolerance. The pitfall is simplifying so hard that edges cross; turn on the option that prevents it.

tasks.want: thin out a track or boundary to a distance tolerance
cut a shape down to a set number of vertices

geometry.validity.summary: Checks that polygons are well formed, and repairs them.
geometry.validity.intro: This group checks a polygon for problems such as crossed or touching edges, duplicate corners, spikes, holes outside the outline, and wrong ring order, says where each one is, and returns a repaired polygon. GIS analysts and developers use it before measuring areas or running overlays. Start with check and repair. A common pitfall is a bow-tie outline with crossed edges, whose area means nothing until it is split into two triangles.

tasks.want: check a polygon and repair it

indexing.intro: Spatial indexes turn a location into a short key you can store, join, and search. This section covers H3 hexagons, S2 cells, geohashes, Plus Codes, and web map tiles, and converts one place between them. Developers and GIS analysts use them to bucket points, join datasets by cell, and plan map caches. If you are not sure which system fits, start with the cross-index tool, which shows one place in each at a matched cell size. Pitfall: every key names an area, not a point, and its size depends on the resolution you choose.

indexing.convert.summary: Moving between indexing systems: one place in each, at resolutions chosen to match a cell size.
indexing.convert.intro: One place written in every indexing system this site supports: H3, S2, geohash, Plus Code, web map tile, Maidenhead, and MGRS. Each is shown at the resolution whose cell is closest to a size you name, with the size the cell really has there. Developers and GIS analysts use it to choose a system or to match resolutions between two datasets. Start with the cross-index tool and a target size such as 150 m. Pitfall: the matches are approximate, because each system steps in its own ratio, so no two cells cover exactly the same ground.

tasks.want: see one place in every indexing system at a matched cell size

indexing.geohash.intro: Geohashes name a rectangle on the map with a short base-32 string, and each added character makes the box smaller. These tools encode and decode geohashes, find a cell's eight neighbors, and list the cells that cover a box or polygon. Developers use them for string keys, prefix searches, and simple spatial bucketing. Start with the encoder, which shows the cell's size and bounds at any length. Pitfall: points just across a cell edge can share no prefix at all, so always search a cell together with its neighbors.

tasks.want: encode or decode a geohash
find a geohash's neighbors
list the geohashes over a box or polygon

indexing.h3.intro: H3 is Uber's hexagonal grid: 16 resolutions, each cell about one seventh the area of its parent, with 12 pentagons at every resolution. These tools index points, inspect cells, walk the hierarchy, search rings and paths, fill polygons, and outline sets of cells. Analysts and developers use H3 to aggregate points, join datasets, and search neighborhoods. Start with the resolution chooser to pick a cell size, then the point-to-cell tool. Pitfall: near a pentagon a cell has five neighbors, not six, so code that expects fixed ring sizes can break.

tasks.want: find the H3 cell for a point, or inspect a cell
choose a resolution
move up or down the hierarchy
find cells around or between cells
do grid arithmetic around an origin cell
fill a polygon with cells
outline a set of cells as a polygon

indexing.plus-code.intro: Plus Codes, also called Open Location Codes, are short codes for places that have no street address, like 87G2C2W9+ for a spot in downtown Pittsburgh. These tools encode a point, decode a code to the area it names, and shorten a code relative to a nearby town. Field teams and developers use them where addresses are missing or unreliable. Start with the encoder. Pitfall: a shortened code only makes sense next to its reference place; without that place, it cannot be turned back into one location.

tasks.want: encode or decode a Plus Code
shorten a Plus Code near a reference place

indexing.s2.summary: S2 cells: a point to a cell id or token at any level, what a cell covers, and the cells across its edges.
indexing.s2.intro: S2 projects a cube onto the sphere and splits each face into four children per level, from level 0 down to level 30, where cells are about 1 cm across. These tools turn a point into a cell id or token, describe what a cell covers, find its edge neighbors across cube faces, and cover a box or circle with cells. Developers use S2 for 64-bit spatial keys and region coverings. Start with the point-to-cell tool. Pitfall: a token and a 64-bit id are two spellings of the same cell, so compare like with like.

tasks.want: turn a point into an S2 cell, or read a token
find the cells around one, including across a cube face
cover a box or a circle with S2 cells

indexing.tile.summary: Web map tiles and ground resolution.
indexing.tile.intro: Web map tiles divide the Web Mercator map into squares named by zoom, x, and y, or by a Bing quadkey. These tools find the tile for a point, give a tile's bounds, list its parent and children, cover a box with tiles, and give meters per pixel and map scale at any zoom. Map developers use them to debug tile URLs and size offline caches. Start with the tile-for-a-point tool, which shows XYZ, TMS, and quadkey at once. Pitfall: TMS counts rows up from the south and XYZ down from the north, so a mixed-up y lands in the wrong hemisphere.

tasks.want: find the tile for a point, or a tile's bounds
know the ground resolution and scale at a zoom
find a tile's parent and children, or the tiles over a box

navigation.intro: These tools find distances, courses, and routes on the Earth, and what can be seen over its curve. Pilots, mariners, drone operators, radio planners, and developers use them for planning and checking. Distances use the WGS 84 ellipsoid, with spherical versions alongside to show the difference. Start with distance between two points, and compare it with the haversine tool to see how far the spherical shortcut drifts on your route.

navigation.geodesic.intro: These tools solve distance and course problems on the Earth: the shortest path between two points on the ellipsoid, the destination from a start, course, and distance, midpoints, waypoints, and where two paths cross, plus the spherical and Vincenty versions for comparison. Pilots, mariners, developers, and GIS analysts use them. Start with distance between two points, and compare it with the haversine tool to see how far the spherical shortcut drifts on your route. The pitfall is trusting the haversine formula for reported distances; it can be off by tenths of a percent.

tasks.want: work on a sphere: great-circle course, destination, or a point part way
find the distance and courses between two points
find where I end up from a start, course, and distance
find points along the way
check whether two lines cross, or find a route's highest point

steps.text: The geodesic tools solve the ellipsoid exactly (Karney's method) and are the ones to use.
Haversine treats the earth as a sphere and can be off by about 0.5%; it is here for comparison with other software.
Vincenty's method is a legacy iteration that can fail near antipodal points; it is here to check older results.

navigation.los.summary: Horizon, line of sight, and radio clearance.
navigation.los.intro: These tools answer line-of-sight questions: how far the horizon is, how far below eye level it lies, whether two raised points can see each other over the Earth's curve, and the Fresnel zone clearance a radio link needs. Radio and antenna planners, drone operators, and mariners use them. Start with distance to the horizon. The pitfall is ignoring refraction; light and radio bend, and the answer depends on which you mean.

tasks.want: know how far the horizon is
check whether two points can see each other
check a radio link's Fresnel clearance

navigation.rhumb.intro: A rhumb line keeps one compass course all the way, and these tools find its course and distance between two points and the destination along a constant course, on the ellipsoid. Mariners and pilots planning constant-heading legs use them. Start with rhumb line distance and course. The pitfall is using a rhumb line for a long east-west route at high latitude, where it can be far longer than the shortest path.

tasks.want: find the distance and course of a rhumb line
find where a constant course takes me

navigation.route.summary: Routes, legs, and the geometry around them.
navigation.route.intro: These tools work with routes and moving objects: legs and totals for a route, cross-track error, the closest point on a route, range rings, fly-by turns, closest point of approach, intercepts, and time, speed, and distance. Pilots, drone operators, and mariners use them for planning. Start with route legs. A pitfall is mixing true and magnetic courses between legs; the legs tool lists both.

tasks.want: find where two courses cross
work out the course to intercept a moving target
total up a route's legs
know how far I am off a route
find when two moving craft pass closest
anticipate a turn at a waypoint
draw range rings around a point

navigation.vector.summary: Distances and angles between points with heights.
navigation.vector.intro: These tools handle vectors and straight-line geometry: 3D distance between two points with heights, look angles from an observer to a target, vector sums and products, and conversion between magnitude and direction and x, y, z components. Drone operators, antenna installers, and students use them. Start with look angles. The pitfall is mixing direction conventions: navigation measures clockwise from north, mathematics counterclockwise from the x axis.

tasks.want: measure the straight-line distance to a drone or aircraft
point an antenna or camera at a target
add vectors or turn a direction into components

raster.intro: Raster tools work on the numbers in one pixel or a small window of a satellite image or elevation model: scaling bands to reflectance, spectral indices such as NDVI, and terrain measures such as slope and ruggedness. They are for checking a formula or a pixel by hand, not for processing whole scenes. Start by scaling a band to reflectance, then compute an index from it. All of the raster tools are still experimental.

raster.index.summary: Spectral indices from surface reflectance: vegetation, water, built-up, and burn severity, each with the paper it comes from.
raster.index.intro: Spectral index tools compute NDVI, EVI, SAVI, the two NDWIs and MNDWI, NDBI, and the burn ratios from band reflectances, each with the paper that defines it, plus band math for an index of your own. Remote sensing analysts, agronomists, and fire and water mappers use them to check a pixel or a formula before running it over a whole scene. Start with NDVI. One pitfall: the formulas expect surface reflectance, roughly 0 to 1, not the digital numbers stored in the file, so scale each band first; the tools flag values that look unscaled.

tasks.want: measure vegetation in a pixel
find water, or measure water in vegetation
map built-up ground or burn severity
write an index of my own over named bands

raster.scale.summary: Turning a band's stored digital numbers into surface reflectance, with each sensor's own scaling.
raster.scale.intro: The scaling tool turns a band's stored digital number into surface reflectance with the sensor's own published scaling: the Sentinel-2 Level-2A offset and quantification value, or the Landsat Collection 2 gain and offset. Anyone computing a spectral index from raw Sentinel-2 or Landsat values needs this step first. One pitfall: Sentinel-2 Level-2A data from processing baseline 04.00 on carry an offset, so reflectance is the digital number minus 1,000, divided by 10,000, and dropping the offset shifts every index.

tasks.want: scale a band to reflectance before computing an index

raster.terrain.summary: What a digital elevation model says about a cell and the ground around it: how steep it is, which way it faces, how broken it is, and where its contours run.
raster.terrain.intro: Terrain tools read a 3 x 3 window of a digital elevation model and describe its center cell: slope, aspect, and hillshade by Horn's method, and the terrain ruggedness index, topographic position index, and roughness. A contour tool turns a whole grid of elevations into contour lines at an interval. GIS analysts, hydrologists, and site planners use them to check a cell by hand or to test the numbers a GIS reports. Start with slope, aspect, and hillshade. One pitfall: on a grid in degrees, a cell is narrower east to west than north to south away from the equator, so its size must be corrected for latitude, which the slope tool does.

tasks.want: find the slope, aspect, and hillshade of a cell
describe how rugged the ground is, and whether a cell is a ridge or a hollow
draw contour lines from a grid of elevations

survey.intro: Calculators for land and construction surveying: coordinate geometry and traverses, horizontal and vertical curves, earthwork volumes, GNSS field work, deeds and legal descriptions, and distance reductions. They are for surveyors, survey technicians, and civil engineers checking field and office work. Most jobs start with the inverse and traverse closure tools in coordinate geometry. Watch grid versus ground: distances between state plane coordinates differ from measured ground distances by the combined factor.

survey.cogo.summary: Coordinate geometry: inverses, forwards, intersections, resection, offset shots, traverses, and areas.
survey.cogo.intro: Coordinate geometry on plane survey coordinates: inverse and forward, intersections, resection, offset shots, station and offset, traverse closure and adjustment, least-squares networks, and area by coordinates. It is for surveyors reducing field work and checking plats. Start with the inverse tool for a bearing and distance, or traverse closure for a loop. Check angular closure before linear closure: the compass and transit rules spread a blunder across every course instead of finding it.

tasks.want: find bearing and distance between two points, or a point from them
locate a point the prism could not sit on
find where two bearings or distances meet
locate my station from three control points
find a point's station and offset from a line, or set one out
check and adjust a traverse, angles and distances
adjust a network by least squares, with error ellipses
find an area from coordinates

survey.curves.intro: Road and rail geometry: horizontal circular curves, spiral transitions, curve staking tables, equal- and unequal-tangent vertical curves, and vertical curve length for sight distance. It is for survey crews staking alignments and engineers checking plans. Start with the circular curve tool or the vertical curve tool. Check whether a degree of curve uses the arc or the chord definition before turning it into a radius, because the two give different curves.

tasks.want: lay out a horizontal curve
lay out a spiral transition
stake out a curve at a station interval
design a vertical curve
size a vertical curve for sight distance

survey.earthwork.summary: Volumes, truck loads, grades, and slope stakes.
survey.earthwork.intro: Earthwork quantities: cut and fill areas at a cross section, volumes by average end area, the prismoidal formula, and a borrow-pit grid, stockpile volumes, swell and shrink with truck loads, grades and side slopes, and slope stakes. It is for survey crews, estimators, and contractors. Start with section areas, then average end area between stations. Label side slopes as H:V or V:H: an unlabeled 3:1 is ambiguous, and the grade tool will not accept one.

tasks.want: find the cut and fill areas of a cross section
find a volume between cross sections or over a grid
account for swell and shrink and count truck loads
convert a grade between percent, degrees, and ratios
set a slope stake at the catch point
check the grades along a profile
measure a stockpile or a simple solid

survey.gnss.summary: GNSS field work: precision budgets, OPUS sessions, and antenna heights.
survey.gnss.intro: GNSS field work: the precision a receiver's millimeters-plus-ppm specification promises over your baseline, planning an NGS OPUS session and naming its RINEX file, reducing a slant antenna height to the antenna reference point, and site localization that fits local coordinates to the grid. It is for surveyors running RTK, PPK, and static sessions. Start with the RTK and PPK precision budget. A slant height measured to the edge of the antenna is not the vertical height to the reference point, so reduce it before processing.

tasks.want: estimate RTK or PPK precision from a receiver's spec
plan an OPUS session and name the RINEX file
turn a slant antenna height into the vertical to the ARP
fit local site coordinates to the grid through control points

survey.land.summary: Deeds, legal descriptions, and old units.
survey.land.intro: Boundary work from the record: reading metes-and-bounds deeds, plotting their calls with closure and area, rotating bearings to a new basis, reading PLSS legal descriptions, converting chains, rods, and varas, and checking relative positional precision under the 2026 ALTA/NSPS standards. Start with the deed parser, then the deed plot. A deed plot shows what the document says, not where the line is on the ground: monuments and calls for adjoiners usually control over bearings and distances, and that is a surveyor's judgment.

tasks.want: check a survey against the ALTA/NSPS precision standard
read a metes-and-bounds deed and plot it
rotate bearings to a new basis
read a PLSS description
convert chains, rods, links, and varas

steps.text: Read the calls out of the deed text: bearings, distances, and curves.
Plot them, check the closure, and find the area.
If the deed's bearings are on a different basis from your survey, rotate them.

survey.reduction.summary: Slope, stadia, and level-run reductions, heights you cannot reach, curvature and refraction, and scale between grid and ground.
survey.reduction.intro: Turning field measurements into usable numbers: slope distance to horizontal, stadia, level runs and their closure, heights you cannot reach, curvature and refraction on long sights, EDM atmospheric and prism corrections, and the combined factor between grid and ground. It is for field crews and office staff reducing raw observations. Start with the slope reduction or the level run. Use ellipsoid height, not sea-level elevation, in the combined factor, and divide a grid area by the combined factor squared to get a ground area.

tasks.want: correct an EDM distance for the air and the prism constant
reduce a slope distance to horizontal and vertical
reduce a stadia reading
find the height of a tower or tree I cannot reach
reduce a level run and check its closure
correct a long sight for curvature and refraction
scale distances between grid and ground

time.intro: Time tools cover clocks and the sun. The time scale group converts between local time, UTC, GPS time, and Julian dates, and logs flight time. The sun group finds sunrise, twilight, the sun's position, and the night periods that US aviation rules use. Pilots, drone operators, and GNSS surveyors each lean on a different part. Every tool takes an explicit UTC offset or time zone and never reads your device's clock or zone, so the same inputs give the same answer anywhere.

time.scale.summary: Time scales, zones, and flight time.
time.scale.intro: Time scale tools convert between the clocks that aviation, GNSS, and astronomy keep: local time and UTC (Zulu), GPS week and seconds, Julian dates and day of year, and flight time in hours and minutes or decimal hours. Pilots use them to turn a local departure time into Zulu and to log block time. GNSS users and surveyors use them to match receiver time to UTC and name RINEX files. Start with local time to UTC, which handles daylight saving gaps and the date change. One pitfall: GPS time runs ahead of UTC by the leap seconds added since 1980, now 18 seconds.

tasks.want: convert local time to UTC, or check a zone's rules
convert between UTC and GPS time
find a Julian date or day of year
log flight time

time.sun.summary: Where the sun is and when it rises and sets.
time.sun.intro: Sun tools find where the sun is and when it rises, sets, and passes through civil, nautical, and astronomical twilight, for any place and date, in local time and Zulu. Pilots use them for the four US aviation nights and night passenger currency. Drone operators use them for Part 107 civil twilight, mapping light, and the sun's hotspot in photos. Start with sunrise, sunset, and twilight. One pitfall: aviation rules define night in different ways, so a landing can be logged as night and still not count toward passenger currency.

tasks.want: check my night passenger currency from my logbook
know sunrise, sunset, and twilight
know when night starts for aviation rules
find the hours of good light for mapping
check whether the sun's hotspot will show in my photos
find the sun's azimuth and elevation

units.intro: Unit converters for the quantities that come up in flying, drone work, surveying, and mapping: length, area, speed, pressure, temperature, fuel, battery charge, and more. Most use exact unit definitions; fuel weight uses a density you can see and change. Pilots, drone operators, surveyors, and developers use them alongside the other tools. If you have a value written with its unit, like 145 kts, start with the quantity normalizer. Pitfall: many units share a name, such as the US survey foot and the international foot, or US and imperial gallons, so check which one your source means.

units.acceleration.intro: Converts acceleration between meters per second squared, feet per second squared, and standard gravity (g). Engineers and drone builders use it for accelerometer ranges, load factors, and vibration limits. Start with the acceleration converter. Pitfall: g here is standard gravity, a fixed defined value, not the gravity at your site, which varies slightly with latitude and height. A sensor that reports in g has already been scaled by that standard value.

units.angle.intro: Converts angles between degrees, radians, gons, arcminutes, arcseconds, milliarcseconds, milliradians, turns, and three kinds of military mil. Surveyors, GIS developers, and anyone reading a compass or a code library use it. Start with the angle converter, or the degrees-to-radians and radians-to-degrees shortcuts for code. Pitfall: "mil" means different things. NATO, Warsaw Pact, and Swedish mils divide a circle into different numbers of parts, and none of them is exactly a milliradian, so check which one your instrument uses.

units.angular-rate.intro: Converts turn and rotation rates: degrees per second or per minute, radians per second, revolutions per minute, and slow rates such as arcseconds or milliarcseconds per year. Drone builders read gyro and motor specs with it, and geodesists use it for plate and frame rotation rates. Start with the angular rate converter. Pitfall: many gyros and code libraries report radians per second while datasheets quote degrees per second. One radian per second is 57.29578 degrees per second, so a mix-up is hard to miss but easy to make.

units.area.intro: Converts areas between square meters, square kilometers, hectares, acres, square feet, square miles, and square nautical miles. Surveyors, farmers, and drone mappers use it for parcels, fields, and survey blocks. Start with the area converter, or the acres and hectares shortcuts. Pitfall: an area factor is the square of a length factor, so applying a length conversion to an area gives the wrong answer. A hectare is a square 100 m on a side.

units.charge.intro: Converts battery charge between milliamp-hours, amp-hours, and coulombs, and to watt-hours at a voltage you state. Drone pilots and builders use it to compare packs and to check limits written in watt-hours. Start with the battery charge converter. Pitfall: charge is not energy. Two packs with the same mAh can hold very different energy at different voltages, so compare packs in watt-hours at their nominal voltage.

units.data-rate.intro: Converts data rates between bits, kilobits, megabits, and gigabits per second. Drone operators use it for video downlinks and telemetry links, and developers for network and storage budgets. Start with the data rate converter. Pitfall: link rates are in bits, but file sizes are usually in bytes, and a byte is 8 bits. Divide a bit rate by 8 before comparing it with a file size, and allow for protocol overhead on top.

units.density.intro: Converts densities between kilograms per cubic meter, grams per cubic centimeter, pounds per US gallon, and pounds per cubic foot. Pilots use it for fuel weight, and surveyors and engineers for soil and material weights. Start with the density converter. Pitfall: pounds per gallon depends on which gallon, and this converter uses the US gallon. Fuel density also changes with temperature, so use a measured value for weight and balance.

units.energy.intro: Converts energy between joules, kilojoules, megajoules, watt-hours, kilowatt-hours, and foot-pounds. Drone operators use it for battery energy and impact energy, and engineers for work and heat. Start with the energy converter. Pitfall: watts and watt-hours are different things. Watts are a rate, like speed; watt-hours are an amount, like distance. A battery holds watt-hours, a motor draws watts, and flight time is the first divided by the second.

units.frequency.intro: Converts frequency between hertz, kilohertz, megahertz, and gigahertz, and converts drift rates in parts per million or per billion per year. Drone operators use it for radio bands, and surveyors and timing engineers for oscillator drift. Start with the frequency converter. Pitfall: a drift in ppm is relative, so the same ppm means a bigger shift at a higher frequency. Convert it to hertz at your own frequency before you compare two parts.

units.fuel.intro: Converts aviation fuel between volume and weight, using a density you enter or a nominal density for avgas 100LL or jet A. Pilots use it for fuel loads, weight and balance, and ordering. Start with the fuel converter. Pitfall: nominal densities are planning values. Real fuel density changes with temperature and batch, so 50 US gallons of 100LL is 300 lb only at the nominal 6 lb per gallon. Use a measured density for weight and balance.

units.length.intro: Converts length and distance between meters, kilometers, feet, US survey feet, inches, yards, statute miles, and nautical miles, with shortcuts for the common pairs. Pilots, surveyors, and developers use it every day. Start with the length converter. Pitfall: the US survey foot and the international foot are not the same. The gap is only 2 ft in 1,000,000 ft, but state plane coordinates run into the millions of feet, so the wrong foot moves a point by feet on the ground.

units.mass.intro: Converts mass between kilograms, grams, pounds, ounces, and metric tonnes. Pilots use it for weight and balance, and drone operators for takeoff mass and payload limits. Start with the mass converter, or the kilograms and pounds shortcuts. Pitfall: a metric tonne, a US short ton, and a UK long ton are three different masses. This converter handles metric tonnes; convert short or long tons through pounds.

units.power.intro: Converts power between watts, kilowatts, and mechanical horsepower (550 foot-pounds-force per second). Pilots compare engine ratings with it, and drone builders use it for motor and battery loads. Start with the power converter. Pitfall: horsepower comes in more than one kind. Metric horsepower is slightly smaller than mechanical horsepower, so check which one an engine or motor rating uses before you convert it.

units.pressure.intro: Converts pressure between inches of mercury, hectopascals, millibars, pascals, kilopascals, bars, psi, millimeters of mercury, and atmospheres. Pilots use it for altimeter settings, and engineers for tire, hydraulic, and weather pressures. Start with the pressure converter, or the inHg and hPa shortcuts. Pitfall: an altimeter setting is not the air pressure at the airport. It is reduced to sea level, so do not use it as station pressure in a density calculation.

units.quantity.intro: Reads a value written with its unit, like 145 kts or 10 gal, and returns it in canonical units: SI, with angles in degrees. Developers use it to clean up mixed-unit data before running other tools, and anyone can use it to check what a unit label means. Start with the quantity normalizer. Pitfall: some unit names are ambiguous. The tool reads gal as US gallons, not imperial gallons, and warns you when it makes a choice like that.

units.slope.intro: Converts a slope between rise over run, percent grade, per mille, and degrees. Surveyors, road and site designers, and drone mappers use it for grades, ramps, and terrain. Start with the slope converter. Pitfall: percent and degrees do not scale together. A 100% grade is a 45° slope, not a vertical wall, and the gap between the two scales widens as slopes get steeper.

units.speed.intro: Converts speed between knots, statute miles per hour, kilometers per hour, meters per second, and feet per second, with shortcuts for the common pairs. Pilots and drone operators use it for airspeed, wind, and groundspeed limits. Start with the speed converter. Pitfall: a knot is one nautical mile per hour, not one statute mile per hour. Weather reports give wind in knots, while many drone apps show mph or m/s, so convert before you compare.

units.temperature.intro: Converts temperature readings between degrees Celsius, degrees Fahrenheit, and kelvins. Pilots use it for outside air temperature and dew point, and everyone else for weather and equipment limits. Start with the temperature converter, or the Celsius and Fahrenheit shortcuts. Pitfall: this converter is for readings. For a change or a deviation, like ISA +15 °C, use the temperature difference converter, or you will add an offset that does not belong.

units.temperature-difference.intro: Converts a change in temperature, not a temperature reading, between degrees Celsius, kelvins, and degrees Fahrenheit. Pilots use it for deviation from the ISA standard temperature and for lapse rates. Start with the temperature difference converter. Pitfall: using the ordinary temperature formula on a difference adds a 32° offset that does not belong. A change of 10 °C is a change of 18 °F, while a reading of 10 °C is 50 °F.

units.time.intro: Converts durations between milliseconds, seconds, minutes, hours, and days. Pilots use it for logbook time, and drone operators and developers for endurance and timing. Start with the time converter. Pitfall: decimal hours are not hours and minutes. 1.5 h is 90 minutes, which is 1 hour 30 minutes, not 1 hour 50 minutes, so convert before you write a decimal time on a clock.

units.vertical-speed.intro: Converts climb and descent rates between feet per minute, meters per second, meters per minute, and feet per second. Pilots use it for climb and descent rates, and drone operators for ascent and descent limits. Start with the vertical speed converter. Pitfall: aircraft instruments show feet per minute, while drone specs often use meters per second, and the same rate looks very different in the two units, so convert before you compare.

units.volume.intro: Converts volume between cubic meters, liters, US gallons, imperial gallons, cubic feet, and cubic yards. Pilots use it for fuel, and surveyors and contractors for earthwork and stockpiles. Start with the volume converter, or the gallons and liters shortcuts. Pitfall: the US gallon and the imperial gallon are different sizes, so check which one your source uses. The shortcuts use US gallons, where one gallon is 3.7854118 liters.
